title: No death detection on the client: a crashed or killed app leaves its CastV2 session, threads and receiver virtual connection open
failure_scenario: An app connects through the connectionless client (zzbm: addListener + connect) or the legacy one (listener in extras), launches a receiver app, and then its process dies (crash, force-stop or LMK). Nothing sends ICastDeviceController.disconnect, and the controller never calls linkToDeath on the listener binder (lines 53 and 72-74). Teardown only happens in notify() (lines 162-169), and only when a later callback fails with DeadObjectException. With an idle device, or a paused receiver app that sends no RECEIVER_STATUS or message on a registered namespace, no callback ever fires. GmsCore then keeps the TLS socket, the reader thread, the heartbeat thread (PING every 5 s) and the session executor thread indefinitely. It also keeps the virtual connection to the receiver app's transportId open. The receiver still counts a connected sender, so receiver apps that shut down when the last sender leaves never stop, and the TV stays on the cast app after the phone app is gone.
evidence: CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:53 `if (listenerWrapper != null) listener = ICastDeviceControllerListener.Stub.asInterface(listenerWrapper.binder)` and :72-74 `override fun addListener(listener) { this.listener = listener }`: no linkToDeath anywhere (grep for linkToDeath/DeathRecipient/binderDied in play-services-cast returns nothing). The only cleanup trigger is notify() :166-169 `catch (e: RemoteException) { ... disconnect() }`. CastChannel.kt:196-198/216-226 keeps answering and sending heartbeats internally, so heartbeat traffic never reaches notify(). BaseService has no per-client unbind hook.
suggested_fix: In the init block and in addListener, register an IBinder.DeathRecipient on listener.asBinder() that calls disconnect(). Unlink it in removeListener/disconnect and when the listener is replaced, and treat a failed linkToDeath (the binder is already dead) as an immediate disconnect.

verdict.reasoning: I traced the path and could not refute it. The listener comes from BinderWrapper at CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:52-53 or from addListener at :72-74. Nothing in play-services-cast calls linkToDeath, and BaseService (play-services-base/core/.../BaseService.java) has no per-client unbind hook. The only automatic teardown is notify() at :162-172: a oneway call to a dead listener throws DeadObjectException, which leads to disconnect(). Heartbeat PING/PONG is handled entirely inside CastChannel.readLoop/heartbeatTick (CastChannel.kt:196-198, 216-226) and never reaches notify(). Receiver messages are only forwarded for an attached app and a registered namespace (CastDeviceSession.kt:294-298). RECEIVER_STATUS only comes on state changes. So after the client process dies, an idle device or a paused receiver app produces no callback. GmsCore then keeps the TLS socket, the CastChannel reader thread, the heartbeat executor (PING every 5 s), the session executor and the app transport's virtual connection. CastMediaRouteController.onRelease, which MediaRouteProviderService calls on client death, does not reach this. It uses its own su.litvak ChromeCast (CastMediaRouteController.java:39, 96-101) and never touches CastDeviceSession. Cleanup only happens if a heartbeat timeout or a receiver message later causes a callback, so it is environment-dependent and can be indefinite while the phone is awake. This is a real resource leak and keeps a sender attached to the receiver app.

title: Session executor thread leaks after a failed connect or a remote disconnect when the client never calls disconnect() (legacy clients never do)
failure_scenario: (a) A legacy client (cast.internal.zzx, listener in extras) connects to an unreachable device or one that fails device auth. CastDeviceSession.connect hits the failure path and calls onConnectionFailed. CastDeviceControllerService:54 answers onPostInit with a non-zero status and a null binder, so the client can never reach the controller. Nothing calls session.disconnect(), so the ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor core thread 'CastDeviceSession-<host>' (core threads never time out) stays parked forever. (b) A legacy client is connected and the Wi-Fi drops. onClosed delivers onDisconnected(7), and the client's zzw.zzb disposes its listener and calls triggerConnectionSuspended(2). From then on zzx.disconnect() short-circuits ('already disposed') and never sends ICastDeviceController.disconnect, and the reconnect creates a new controller, so the old session's executor thread is never shut down. Every failed attempt or network drop leaks one thread in the persistent GmsCore process.
evidence: CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:115-128 onConnectionFailed -> onConnectResult only calls initCallback/notify. :130-133 onDisconnected only unregisters and calls notify. Neither calls session.disconnect(). CastDeviceSession.kt:95-99 failure path: `channel = null; callbacks.onConnectionFailed(...)` with no executor.shutdown(). Only disconnect() at :105-111 shuts the executor down. CastDeviceControllerService.java:52-57: on statusCode != 0 it passes a null binder and only calls controller.disconnect() on RemoteException. Client zzx.disconnect(): `if (zzwVar == null || zzwVar.zzq() == null) { logger.d("already disposed, so short-circuiting"); return; }`. zzw.zzb(i): `zzx zzxVarZzq = zzq(); ... if (i != 0) zzxVarZzq.triggerConnectionSuspended(2);`.
suggested_fix: Tear the session down when the connection is terminally gone: call disconnect() (or session.disconnect()) in onConnectResult when statusCode != 0 on the legacy init path, and in onDisconnected after notifying the listener. A legacy client cannot reuse the controller after either event, and a connectionless client gets a fresh controller on the next connect. Alternatively, let CastDeviceSession shut down its own executor in the connect-failure path and in onClosed.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed against the code and the 22.3.1 client. (a) CastDeviceSession.connect fails at :95-99, where it sets channel = null and calls onConnectionFailed without shutting the executor down. CastDeviceControllerImpl.onConnectResult (:117-128) only calls initCallback. CastDeviceControllerService.java:52-58 then delivers onPostInit(status, null) and only disconnects on RemoteException. The client gets a null binder, so it can never call disconnect. ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(1) (CastDeviceSession.kt:74) keeps its core thread parked in DelayedWorkQueue.take(). The thread keeps its Worker and executor reachable, so finalize/GC never reclaims it. (b) onClosed -> onDisconnected(7) (CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:130-133) only notifies the listener. In the client, zzw.zzb calls zzq(), which nulls its zzx reference, then triggerConnectionSuspended(2). zzx.disconnect() then hits `zzwVar.zzq() == null` -> 'already disposed, so short-circuiting' and never sends ICastDeviceController.disconnect. The reconnect builds a new zzw and a new GetServiceRequest, so a new controller is created. The old session's executor thread is never shut down. Reader and heartbeat threads do exit in CastChannel.shutdown, so each event leaks exactly one parked thread plus the controller and listener proxy. The connectionless client does not leak here: zzbl.zzb unregisters its listener (zzC -> zzas -> removeListener -> disconnect). The leak is real but small per event and grows with each failed legacy connect or each network drop, so the severity is low. The alternative fix (shutting the executor down inside CastDeviceSession on failure or close) is unsafe. CastDeviceSession.connect is written to reconnect a closed channel (:86-92), and a shut-down executor silently drops later posts (post() :326), so a connectionless client that retries connect() on the same controller would hang. The fix should stay limited to the legacy path.

title: Legacy reconnect ignores last_application_id/last_session_id and reports 0 ('app still attached') when it is not
failure_scenario: A legacy Cast.API (GoogleApiClient) app launches a receiver app. zzw.zze stores the app id and session id via zzT/zzU. The connection drops: microG sends onDisconnected(7), and the client calls triggerConnectionSuspended(CAUSE_NETWORK_LOST), after which GoogleApiClient reconnects. The new GetServiceRequest extras carry 'last_application_id'/'last_session_id' (zzx.getGetServiceRequestExtraArgs). The client treats status 0 as 'rejoined, app still running' and status 2300 as 'app no longer running' (connection hint EXTRA_APP_NO_LONGER_RUNNING). microG ignores both extras, opens a bare connection and returns 0 without attaching to the app's transport. The app resumes sending media/custom messages without calling joinApplication. Every sendMessage then fails with 2005 (CastDeviceSession.sendToApplication: application == null), and the app never learns that it has to rejoin, so casting is stuck after any network blip.
evidence: Client zzx.getGetServiceRequestExtraArgs: `bundle.putString("last_application_id", str); ... bundle.putString("last_session_id", str2);`. zzx.onPostInitHandler: `if (i == 0 || i == 2300) {...} if (i == 2300) { this.zzz.putBoolean(Cast.EXTRA_APP_NO_LONGER_RUNNING, true); i = 0; }`. microG CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:49-56 reads only the CastDevice and 'listener'. CastDeviceControllerService.java:52-54 forwards the bare connect status. CastDeviceSession.kt:212 `channel == null || app == null -> onSendMessageFailure(..., STATUS_APPLICATION_NOT_RUNNING)`.
suggested_fix: On the legacy (listener-in-extras) path, read last_application_id/last_session_id. After the channel connects, run GET_STATUS and joinApplication(lastAppId, lastSessionId) before calling onPostInit. Answer 0 if the join succeeds and 2300 (APPLICATION_NOT_RUNNING) if the app is gone.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. In the 22.3.1 client, zzx.getGetServiceRequestExtraArgs puts last_application_id and last_session_id after zzw.zze has stored them via zzT/zzU. zzx.onPostInitHandler maps 2300 to EXTRA_APP_NO_LONGER_RUNNING plus success, and treats 0 as a plain reconnect. zzx never calls joinApplication itself on reconnect. The legacy Cast.API pattern (CastHelloText, CCL onConnectivityRecovered) only re-registers message callbacks and then sends. grep shows the series never reads last_application_id/last_session_id (only Cast.java:59 defines the hint constant). CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:49-56 reads only the device and listener, and the service at :54 forwards the bare connect status 0. After the reconnect, CastDeviceSession.application is null. sendMessage then fails with 2005 (CastDeviceSession.kt:212), and receiver-app messages are dropped (:294). The app is never told to rejoin. This is a contract gap with the real legacy client and breaks control after any network drop. It only affects legacy GoogleApiClient Cast.API apps and the user can recover by reconnecting manually, so the severity is low.

title: Legacy client that disconnects while the connect is in progress leaves an orphaned, connected CastV2 session
failure_scenario: A legacy GoogleApiClient (zzx) binds with a listener in its extras, so handleServiceRequest defers onPostInit until the TLS connect and device auth finish, which can take up to about 20 s. If the app disconnects the GoogleApiClient in that window (for example, the user deselects the route), GmsClient unbinds and drops the stale onPostInit for the old connection id. The deferred callback at line 54 still succeeds because the client process is alive, so no RemoteException is raised and controller.disconnect() at line 57 never runs. The controller binder never reaches the client, so the client can never call disconnect. The session stays connected with 5 s heartbeats and three threads for the life of the client process, and the listener stays alive, so notify() never trips.
evidence: CastDeviceControllerService.java:52-58: `controller.connectBeforeInit(statusCode -> { try { callback.onPostInitCompleteWithConnectionInfo(statusCode, statusCode == 0 ? controller : null, info); } catch (RemoteException e) { ... controller.disconnect(); } ...})`. Cleanup is tied only to the IGmsCallbacks call throwing. Client zzx creates a fresh zzw and connection id per getRemoteService, so a result for an abandoned connection attempt is discarded.
suggested_fix: Link to death on the IGmsCallbacks binder and on the listener. Also bound the orphan case, for example by tearing the session down if no ICastDeviceController call arrives within a timeout after a deferred onPostInit, or by linking the session's lifetime to the listener with F1's death recipient plus an explicit timeout.

verdict.reasoning: The path holds, but the window is narrow. On the legacy path, onPostInit is deferred until CastDeviceSession.connect finishes (TCP connect, TLS and device auth, with a 10 s connect timeout and a 10 s soTimeout). If the app disconnects the GoogleApiClient in that window, zzx.disconnect() runs zzw.zzq(), which succeeds because the listener is not yet disposed. getService() then throws IllegalStateException because the client is not connected, the exception is caught, and super.disconnect() unbinds. Nothing reaches GmsCore. When the connect then succeeds, IGmsCallbacks.onPostInitCompleteWithConnectionInfo (two-way, client alive) returns normally, and BaseGmsClient discards the stale-connection-id result without touching the binder. So the RemoteException branch at CastDeviceControllerService.java:55-57 never runs. The disposed zzw stub stays alive in the client process because GmsCore holds its proxy, so every notify() succeeds silently and the RemoteException teardown in CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:166-169 never fires. The session stays connected to receiver-0 with 5 s heartbeats and three threads until the client process dies, and with the current code even past that (F1). A later network drop closes the socket but leaks the executor (F2b). The window is short for a responsive device, the orphan has no app transport attached, and once F1 is fixed it is bounded by the client process lifetime, so the severity is low. No per-client binder signal exists for an abandoned but live client. The deterministic hook is service destruction: GmsClientSupervisor keeps the service bound while any client is connected, so a bound-only CastDeviceControllerService is only destroyed once no client holds it, and at that point every remaining controller is orphaned.

title: launchApplication decides between join and LAUNCH before the receiver status has arrived, so relaunchIfRunning=false is ignored on a fresh connection
failure_scenario: 1. A receiver app is already running, for example started by another phone. 2. A client starts a new CastSession. microG's CastSessionImpl.onConnected calls launchApplication(appId, new LaunchOptions()), so relaunchIfRunning is false. 3. In CastDeviceSession.connect (lines 101-102), onConnected() is sent to the client first and the GET_STATUS request is written right after it. 4. The client's launchApplication then comes back through the app main looper, the in-process dynamite call and a oneway binder call. That round trip normally takes a few ms, while the GET_STATUS reply from a LAN receiver takes tens of ms. So the launch task usually runs while receiverStatus is still null. 5. Line 118 then finds no running app and sends {type:LAUNCH}. Play services would have joined the running app and reported wasLaunched=false. microG instead issues a LAUNCH for an app that is already running and reports wasLaunched=true (line 130). On a receiver that restarts the app on LAUNCH, this replaces the existing session of the other sender. The join branch at line 119 effectively only works when the status reply wins the race.
evidence: Lines 86-103: connect() calls callbacks.onConnected() before requestReceiver(GET_STATUS). receiverStatus is only set when the reply is processed in handleReceiverMessage (line 260). Line 118: `val running = receiverStatus?.applications?.firstOrNull { it.appId == appId }`. When receiverStatus is null, running is null and the code falls through to the LAUNCH request at lines 123-125, whatever relaunchIfRunning is. joinApplication (lines 141-152) avoids this by issuing GET_STATUS first and deciding in the reply.
suggested_fix: When !relaunchIfRunning, do what joinApplication does: send GET_STATUS (or wait for the GET_STATUS already in flight from connect) and choose attach or LAUNCH in the reply callback, instead of reading a receiverStatus that may still be null. Also clear receiverStatus in onClosed so a later decision never uses status from a previous connection.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by tracing the code. In CastDeviceSession.connect (CastDeviceSession.kt:101-102), callbacks.onConnected() runs before the GET_STATUS write. receiverStatus is only set when that reply comes back: the reader thread posts onMessage, which calls handleReceiverMessage at line 260. On the client side, ICastDeviceControllerListener is oneway, so onConnected does not block. The 22.3.1 client stub cast.zzbl.zzc (binder code 14 = onConnectedWithResult) then posts to zzK() (a Handler), runs the zzp listeners, and the framework CastSession calls ICastSession.onConnected. That is an in-process call into microG's CastSessionImpl.onConnected (CastSessionImpl.java:64-68), which uses new LaunchOptions(), so relaunchIfRunning is false. It then calls ICastConnectionController.launchApplication, which goes through zzbm.zzg, then doWrite, then the oneway zzah.zzn, and becomes a post into the session executor. Nothing orders this launch task after the GET_STATUS reply. If the launch task runs first, line 118 sees a null receiverStatus, skips the join branch and sends LAUNCH (lines 123-125). The reply to that LAUNCH then goes through attachApplication(launched, true) at line 130, so the client gets wasLaunched=true for an app that was already running. Play services treats relaunchIfRunning=false as join-if-running. The legacy client's onPostInitHandler status 2300 / EXTRA_APP_NO_LONGER_RUNNING shows that real GmsCore knows the receiver app state before it reports the connection complete. Common CastV2 senders such as pychromecast handle exactly this case: if the status is unknown they request status first, and a forced re-LAUNCH relaunches the app. A common case is a session ended with 'disconnect' rather than 'stop casting', followed by a new session. Whether it happens depends on timing, but the code has no ordering that guarantees the join path, and the wasLaunched flag and the extra LAUNCH are wrong whenever the race is lost. Casting itself does not fail, so the severity is medium, not high. Secondary point: receiverStatus is never cleared in onClosed, so a later connect() on the same session could decide from stale status. The fix below covers that too.

title: A failed connect on the legacy (listener-in-extras) path never shuts down the CastDeviceSession executor, leaking one thread plus the session and controller per attempt
failure_scenario: 1. An app uses the deprecated GoogleApiClient Cast.API client (cast.internal.zzx). getGetServiceRequestExtraArgs puts a BinderWrapper "listener" into the extras, so handleServiceRequest takes the connectBeforeInit path. 2. The device is unreachable, the TLS handshake or device auth fails, or auth times out. CastChannel.connect throws, and CastDeviceSession.connect (lines 95-99) sets channel=null and calls onConnectionFailed. 3. The init callback sends onPostInitCompleteWithConnectionInfo(statusCode!=0, null, info) and returns. Nothing calls controller.disconnect() or session.disconnect(), and the client never gets a binder it could call disconnect on. 4. The ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(1) created at CastDeviceSession.kt:74 already started its core thread for the connect task. Core threads never time out, so the thread "CastDeviceSession-<host>" stays parked forever. Its ThreadFactory lambda captures the session, which keeps the controller reachable through `callbacks`. Each retry by GoogleApiClient adds another permanent thread to the GmsCore process.
evidence: CastDeviceControllerService.java lines 52-58: the lambda only calls controller.disconnect() on RemoteException; when statusCode != 0 it just returns null as the binder. CastDeviceSession.kt line 74: `ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(1) { Thread(it, "CastDeviceSession-$host") ... }`. The only executor.shutdown() is in disconnect() at line 110. The connect failure branch at lines 95-99 does not shut the executor down. Legacy client: gaar/jadx-play-services-cast/.../cast/internal/zzx.java:163 `bundle.putParcelable("listener", new BinderWrapper(this.zzm))`.
suggested_fix: In the connectBeforeInit callback, call controller.disconnect() whenever statusCode != 0, not only on RemoteException. Alternatively, have CastDeviceSession shut its executor down after reporting onConnectionFailed when it was created only for that connect attempt.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. The 22.3.1 legacy GoogleApiClient client cast.internal.zzx.getGetServiceRequestExtraArgs (zzx.java:163) puts a BinderWrapper "listener" into the extras. So CastDeviceControllerImpl.hasInitialListener is true, and CastDeviceControllerService.java:52 takes the connectBeforeInit path. Suppose CastChannel.connect throws, for example because the receiver is unreachable, the TCP or TLS connect times out, or the receiver returns a device auth error. Then CastDeviceSession.connect (kt:95-99) sets channel=null and calls onConnectionFailed. onConnectResult skips registry registration and invokes initCallback. The lambda sends onPostInitCompleteWithConnectionInfo(statusCode, null, info) and returns. controller.disconnect() is only reached on RemoteException. The client receives no binder, so it can never call disconnect (zzx.disconnect needs getService()). The ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(1) at kt:74 already started its core worker thread in execute()/ensurePrestart. Core threads do not time out (allowCoreThreadTimeOut is false), and the only executor.shutdown() is in disconnect() at kt:110. The thread "CastDeviceSession-<host>" therefore parks in DelayedWorkQueue.take() forever. Its Worker references the executor, so the executor can never be finalized or shut down. The result is one permanent thread per failed legacy connect attempt in the GmsCore process, plus whatever the thread factory lambda captures. Only the deprecated Cast.API GoogleApiClient path is affected. The CAF client (zzbm) uses addListener+connect and disconnects after a failed onConnectedWithResult. Each leak is only one parked thread, so the severity is low, not medium.

title: No death link on the client listener: when a client process dies, the TLS channel, heartbeat, reader and session threads stay open until a later receiver event happens to fail a notify
failure_scenario: 1. A client connects (connect() followed by onConnectedWithResult(0)) and may attach to an app. 2. The client process is killed, for example swiped away or by LMK, without calling disconnect() or removeListener(). 3. Nothing in GmsCore notices, because neither addListener nor the extras listener calls linkToDeath. 4. CastChannel's heartbeat thread keeps sending PING every 5 s and the receiver keeps answering PONG, so the heartbeat timeout never fires. The TLS socket, the reader and heartbeat threads, and the session executor thread stay alive, and the receiver keeps a connected sender-0 virtual connection. Cleanup only happens if some later RECEIVER_STATUS or app message causes notify() to hit DeadObjectException (lines 162-169). On an idle receiver, or with a paused app that produces no status changes, that can be never.
evidence: addListener (lines 72-74) and the init block (line 53) store the ICastDeviceControllerListener without calling asBinder().linkToDeath. The only automatic teardown is the RemoteException branch in notify() (lines 166-169), which runs only when a callback is delivered. CastChannel.heartbeatTick (CastChannel.kt:216-226) keeps the connection alive as long as the receiver answers.
suggested_fix: When a listener is set (in the init block and in addListener), call listener.asBinder().linkToDeath { disconnect() }. Unlink it in removeListener/disconnect.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. Nothing in the series calls linkToDeath. CastDeviceControllerImpl stores the listener in the init block (kt:53, from the extras BinderWrapper) and in addListener (kt:72-74) without a death recipient. BaseService has no unbind or death handling, and CastDeviceControllerService does not override onDestroy or onUnbind. CastMediaRouteController does not touch CastDeviceSession or CastChannelRegistry. When the client process is killed, nothing calls disconnect/removeListener on the controller. CastChannel.heartbeatTick (CastChannel.kt:216-226) sends PING every 5 s, and the receiver's PONG updates lastReceived, so the 20 s heartbeat timeout never fires. As a result the TLS socket, the reader thread, the heartbeat executor thread, the session executor thread and the CastChannelRegistry entry all stay alive, and the receiver keeps sender-0 virtual connections to receiver-0 and to the app transport. Cleanup only happens in notify()'s RemoteException branch (kt:166-169). That branch needs a later RECEIVER_STATUS, or a message on a registered namespace, to hit the dead binder; a oneway transaction to a dead process does throw DeadObjectException. An idle receiver produces no such event, so the leak can last indefinitely. Because the receiver keeps a connected sender, it also misses the sender disconnect. The leak is bounded per dead client and needs no special inputs, so the severity is low.

title: ReconnectionServiceImpl never stops itself when the session ends with a non-zero reason, so the app's started ReconnectionService leaks
failure_scenario: An app uses the 22.3.1 client with the default CastOptions (enableReconnectionService=true, CastOptions.Builder zzg=true) and loads media. On every media status update, client media/internal/zzs.zzd() calls zzs(true), which calls context.startService(ReconnectionService). microG's onStartCommand sees a connected session and returns START_STICKY. Then the receiver application goes away while the session is still up: the user stops it from the TV or Google Home, another sender stops it, or the Default Media Receiver idles out. CastDeviceSession.handleReceiverMessage/onTransportClosed (CastDeviceSession.kt:267/309) then reports onApplicationDisconnected(2005). On the client, cast.zzbl.zzi passes it to framework.zzw.onApplicationDisconnected(2005), then CastSession.zzf(2005), then media.internal.zzs.zzb(2005). That code calls zzt() (context.stopService) only when i == 0, so the client never stops the service. The same happens on the CastSessionImpl.onFailure path, which calls closeConnection(statusCode != 0): ICastConnectionController code 4 goes to zzv.zze(i), then CastSession.zzf(i). After the session ends there are no more status updates and no more startService calls, so onStartCommand never runs again. ReconnectionServiceImpl registers no session listener and never calls stopSelf. The started service stays up with no session and keeps the app process alive in the background. On pre-O devices and in apps targeting below 26 this lasts indefinitely; elsewhere it lasts until the system kills or idles it. With START_STICKY, a kill also restarts the process. The client clearly relies on the module to stop the service on non-zero-reason ends, because its own stop path only handles reason 0.
evidence: ReconnectionServiceImpl.java:28-32 drops the sessionManager listener opportunity and ignores discoveryManager. The only stop logic is the one-shot check at lines 46-52: `if (!hasActiveSession()) { service.stopSelf(startId); return START_NOT_STICKY; } return Service.START_STICKY;`. onCreate (41-43) and onDestroy (61-63) only log. Client 22.3.1, media/internal/zzs.java:159-161: `zzr(); if (i == 0) { zzt(); }`, where zzt() at lines 525-532 is the only stopService(ReconnectionService). zzs.zzb(i) is reached only from CastSession.zzf(i) (CastSession.java:370-371), which is called from zzw.onApplicationDisconnected(i) and zzv.zze(i) (closeConnection). microG sends non-zero codes on both paths: CastDeviceSession.kt:267/309 (STATUS_APPLICATION_NOT_RUNNING=2005) and CastSessionImpl.java:104-114 (closeConnection(statusCode)).
suggested_fix: In onCreate, register an ISessionManagerListener.Stub on the SessionManagerImpl (addSessionManagerListener). Call service.stopSelf() from onSessionEnded, onSessionStartFailed and onSessionResumeFailed, and also when onStartCommand finds no active session. Remove the listener in onDestroy. Optionally return START_NOT_STICKY, since microG does not reconnect from this service, so a killed process is not restarted only to stop again.

verdict.reasoning: I could not refute it. I traced the path in the review tree and in the decompiled 22.3.1 client. (1) The client starts the service with zzs.zzd(), which calls zzs(true) and then context.startService(ReconnectionService) on every media status while a media session is attached (zzs.java:193-196). Default CastOptions.Builder.zzg=true (CastOptions.java:103), and default CastMediaOptions carries NotificationOptions and MediaIntentReceiver, so zzs.zza attaches. (2) While connected, our onStartCommand (ReconnectionServiceImpl.java:46-52) returns START_STICKY. (3) microG ends sessions with non-zero codes. CastDeviceSession.handleReceiverMessage and onTransportClosed call onApplicationDisconnected(2005) unless the stop was self-requested. CastDeviceControllerImpl.kt:147 forwards that to the client listener, and client zzw.onApplicationDisconnected(i) calls CastSession.zzf(i), which calls zzs.zzb(i). Separately, CastSessionImpl.onFailure (CastSessionImpl.java:104-115) calls closeConnection(statusCode), which reaches client zzv.zze(i), then CastSession.zzf(i). (4) zzs.zzb only calls zzt() (stopService) when i == 0 (zzs.java:159-161). It also sets zzp=null and zzt=false, so zzd() returns early after that and no further startService happens. The zzn retry runnable is posted only when startService has thrown, which means the service was never started. (5) No other client class stops the service. I grepped the client: ReconnectionService is referenced only in zzs, zzaq/zzar (the proxy) and zzay (the loader). (6) Our module registers no listener, ignores discoveryManager, and onCreate/onDestroy only log, so nothing calls stopSelf. The started service therefore stays up with no session. The constructor receives the sessionManager, and the client's own stop path only handles reason 0, which shows the module is expected to watch for session end. Severity is lower than reported. On API 26+ with targetSdk >= 26, which covers all current Play apps, the system stops idle background services about a minute after the app goes to the background. While the app is in the foreground the leak does nothing harmful. If the process is killed, the START_STICKY restart runs onStartCommand, which finds no session and stops itself. The leak is unbounded only on API 19-25 devices (androidMinSdk=19) or for legacy-target apps, where it keeps the process at service priority. It causes no crash and no cast failure.

title: Full-size decode with 0x0 hints can throw OutOfMemoryError, which escapes the catch and crashes the client app
failure_scenario: The 22.3.1 client builds most of its image loaders with `new zzb(context)`, which means ImageHints(-1,0,0). That covers the media-session artwork loaders zzj/zzk in media.internal.zzs and the UIMediaController image bindings internal.cast.zzcx/zzda used by MiniControllerFragment. So newFetchBitmapTaskImplWithContext receives targetWidth = targetHeight = 0. FetchBitmapTaskImpl.decode() then skips inSampleSize and decodes the whole image (line 130). Take a large image under the 2 MB download cap, such as a 4000x4000 or 6000x4000 JPEG from a photo-casting app, on API 19-25, where bitmap pixels live on the Java heap. That needs 64-96 MB, and on API 19-22 the in-process Bitmap parcel back to the client adds a second heap copy. BitmapFactory throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError. fetchBitmap catches only IOException | RuntimeException (line 51). The dynamite module runs in the app process and the call is a local Binder.transact, so the Error goes straight into the client's AsyncTask zzd.doInBackground, which catches only RemoteException. AsyncTask's FutureTask.done() then rethrows it as RuntimeException("An error occurred while executing doInBackground()") on the pool thread, and the app process crashes.
evidence: FetchBitmapTaskImpl.java:51 `} catch (IOException | RuntimeException e) {`. decode() at lines 118-131 samples only `if (targetWidth > 0 && targetHeight > 0)`, otherwise `BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray(data, 0, data.length, options)` runs at full size. Client: media/internal/zzb.java:31-33 `this(context, new ImageHints(-1, 0, 0))` and lines 50-51 `new zzd(this.zza, 0, 0, ...)`. media/internal/zzs.java builds `new zzb(this.zzc)` for zzj/zzk, and internal/cast/zzcx.java:37 and zzda.java:52 do `new zzb(context.getApplicationContext())`. zzd.doInBackground (zzd.java:41-46) catches only RemoteException.
suggested_fix: Catch OutOfMemoryError in fetchBitmap and return null. Also bound the decode when no target is given: decode bounds first and pick an inSampleSize that keeps the result under a fixed pixel budget, such as the screen size or about 2048 px on the long edge, in the 0x0 case as well.

verdict.reasoning: The code path holds; how often it triggers depends on the device. (1) The client's media-session artwork loaders zzs.zzj and zzs.zzk (zzs.java:110-112), and the UI bindings in internal/cast/zzcx.java:37 and zzda.java:52, use new zzb(context), which means ImageHints(-1,0,0). zzb.zzb() then builds new zzd(ctx, 0, 0, false, 2097152L, 5, 333, 10000) (zzb.java:50-51). As a result, FetchBitmapTaskImpl gets targetWidth = targetHeight = 0 for every media item with artwork, because the media session is enabled by default. (2) With 0x0 hints, decode() skips sampling and the post-scale step (FetchBitmapTaskImpl.java:120, 130-131), so it decodes at full resolution. The only limit is the 2 MB download cap, which bounds compressed size, not pixel dimensions. A 2 MB JPEG can be 8-12 MP (32-48 MB in ARGB_8888), and a PNG with flat areas can be far larger. (3) On API 19-25, bitmap pixels live on the Java heap. Then Bitmap.writeToParcel/createFromParcel through the in-process reply parcel allocates another heap copy on the client side. (4) The module runs in the app process. The client's proxy calls Binder.transact on the local FetchBitmapTaskImpl, which runs onTransact directly with no catch, so an OutOfMemoryError from BitmapFactory passes through `catch (IOException | RuntimeException e)` at line 51 and reaches client zzd.doInBackground. That method catches only RemoteException (zzd.java:41-46). AsyncTask's WorkerRunnable rethrows it, and FutureTask.done() throws RuntimeException("An error occurred while executing doInBackground()") on the pool thread, which kills the app. The trigger is a large-dimension image of at most 2 MB on a pre-O device with a limited heap. That is uncommon for typical album art (usually 1280x720 or smaller), but photo-casting apps that put the photo URL in MediaMetadata images hit it. On API 26+ the pixels are native and OOM is unlikely. Catching OutOfMemoryError alone is not enough, because the client-side Bitmap.CREATOR copy can still fail outside the module. Bounding the decode is the substantive fix.

title: removeSessionManagerListener/removeCastStateListener never remove anything, so listeners pile up and leak
failure_scenario: An app follows the standard pattern from the CastVideos sample: addSessionManagerListener(l, CastSession.class) in onResume and removeSessionManagerListener(l, CastSession.class) in onPause. Google's own ExpandedControllerActivity does the same, and UIMediaController.dispose() removes in onDestroy. Each call goes through SessionManager.addSessionManagerListener / removeSessionManagerListener, which wrap the listener in a fresh client binder (`new zzbh(listener, cls)`). The module stub turns every incoming binder into a new ISessionManagerListener.Stub.Proxy. The client class zzbh implements the obfuscated zzaz, not microG's ISessionManagerListener, so asInterface always builds a new Proxy, and AIDL proxies compare by identity. HashSet.remove(listener) therefore never finds a match. After N pause/resume cycles the set holds N proxies for the same app listener. onSessionStarted then reaches the app N times: in CastVideos, LocalPlayerActivity.onApplicationConnected calls loadRemoteMedia N times and starts N ExpandedControlsActivity instances. Listeners belonging to paused or destroyed Activities keep receiving callbacks and keep those Activities alive (a memory leak). CastContext.removeCastStateListener has the same problem through `new zzaa(listener)`, which is handled at line 112.
evidence: SessionManagerImpl.java:96-103 and 105-113 add and remove the raw ISessionManagerListener / ICastStateListener objects in a HashSet. In the client, decompiled SessionManager.removeSessionManagerListener does `this.zzb.zzg(new zzbh(sessionManagerListener, cls))` and SessionManager.zzc does `this.zzb.zzi(new zzaa(castStateListener))`. Both create a new wrapper per call. zzbh.zzb() and zzaa.zzb() (getWrappedThis, code 1) return ObjectWrapper.wrap(<user listener>). That wrapped object is the only stable identity the module can compare on.
suggested_fix: Store each listener together with ObjectWrapper.unwrap(listener.getWrappedThis()), the app's own listener object. In remove*, drop every entry whose unwrapped object is the same (==) as the one being removed. In add*, skip a listener whose unwrapped object is already registered. Apply the same change to castStateListeners. Doing it for visibilityListeners (CastContextImpl:258-266) and DiscoveryManagerImpl listeners as well keeps them consistent.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed against the decompiled client. SessionManager.addSessionManagerListener calls zzb.zzf(new zzbh(listener, cls)), which is binder code 2 (AIDL addSessionManagerListener = 1). removeSessionManagerListener calls zzb.zzg(new zzbh(listener, cls)), which is code 3. SessionManager.zzb and zzc, used by CastContext.add/removeCastStateListener, do zzh/zzi(new zzaa(listener)), codes 4 and 5. Every call therefore passes a new Binder. The module is in-process, so readStrongBinder returns that zzbh/zzaa object. microG's AGP-generated ISessionManagerListener.Stub.asInterface gets back an IInterface that is not an instanceof microG's ISessionManagerListener (zzbh implements the obfuscated zzaz), so it builds a new Proxy. Proxy keeps Object identity equals. HashSet.remove at SessionManagerImpl.java:102 and :112 therefore never matches. Binder equality would not help either, because the client sends a different binder each time. Google's own library hits this in normal use: ExpandedControllerActivity adds in onResume and removes in onPause, and UIMediaController adds in its constructor and removes in dispose(), which covers MiniControllerFragment in every Activity. The base already had these add/remove bodies, but it never dispatched session events. With this series, onSessionStarted/onSessionEnded and onCastStateChanged reach every accumulated proxy (lines 305, 316-419). Each zzbh strongly holds the app listener, often an Activity inner class, and the HashSet lives for the whole process, so each destroyed Activity (including on rotation) leaks and keeps getting callbacks. A listener added again after N pause/resume cycles receives each event N+1 times. The fix works because both wrappers' getWrappedThis (zzbh.zzb / zzaa.zzb, code 1) return ObjectWrapper.wrap(user listener), and microG's ObjectWrapper.unwrap reads foreign wrappers by reflection, as CastContextImpl already does for the Context. visibilityListeners does not need the change: the client adds exactly one internal listener, and CastContext.add/removeAppVisibilityListener are no-ops in 22.3.1. DiscoveryManagerImpl listeners are never notified, so they only cause a minor retention.

title: Visibility counter is off by one in the usual setup, so active discovery never stops in background
failure_scenario: In the documented integration, the app calls CastContext.getSharedInstance(this) from Activity.onCreate (as the CastVideos sample does) or from Application.onCreate. The module constructor then runs on the main thread, and runOnMainThread executes trackApplicationVisibility synchronously. That registers the lifecycle callbacks and hard-codes startedActivities = 1 before the creating activity's onStart. onStart then still reaches the new callback (Application.dispatchActivityStarted collects callbacks at dispatch time), so the count becomes 2. When the user leaves the app, onActivityStopped only brings it back to 1 and never to 0. setApplicationVisible(false) is never called and setActiveDiscovery(false) never runs. The MediaRouter callback keeps CALLBACK_FLAG_REQUEST_DISCOVERY for the rest of the process's life. GmsCore's CastMediaRouteProvider.onDiscoveryRequestChanged keeps discoveryWanted=true and NSD/mDNS discovery runs indefinitely while the app sits cached in background (battery and network drain). onAppEnteredBackground is also never sent to the client.
evidence: CastContextImpl.java:229-233: `registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks(lifecycleCallbacks); ... startedActivities = 1; setApplicationVisible(true);`. The comment there assumes the activity 'was already started', which is false when the call comes from onCreate. Line 206 only reports background when `--startedActivities == 0`. Lines 172 and 175-188 tie the discovery flag to applicationVisible.
suggested_fix: Do not assume an activity is already started. Start with startedActivities = 0 and applicationVisible = true. In onActivityStopped, decrement only if the count is above 0, and switch to background whenever the count is 0 after the stop. That covers both registration before onStart and registration after it. Alternatively, derive the initial state from ActivityManager.getMyMemoryState(): importance <= IMPORTANCE_VISIBLE means visible.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. In the decompiled client, CastContext.getSharedInstance(Context) is checkMainThread and synchronously calls new CastContext, then internal.cast.zzay.zza, then newCastContextImpl. The CastContextImpl constructor therefore runs on main, and runOnMainThread (line 135-141) runs R inline. When this happens in Activity.onCreate (the documented pattern and the CastVideos sample) or in Application.onCreate, line 229 registers the callbacks and line 232 sets startedActivities=1 before any onStart. Application.dispatchActivityStarted collects callbacks at dispatch time, so the new callback also gets onActivityStarted and the count reaches 2. When the user leaves, onActivityStopped (line 206) only brings it to 1, so setApplicationVisible(false) and setActiveDiscovery(false) (lines 236-239) never run. The client cannot compensate: its IDiscoveryManager proxy (cast.framework.zzao) only implements getWrappedThis (code 5) and never calls start/stopDiscovery. The MediaRouter callback keeps CALLBACK_FLAG_REQUEST_DISCOVERY, androidx MediaRouter keeps a non-null discovery request for the GmsCore provider service, and CastMediaRouteProvider.onDiscoveryRequestChanged (CastMediaRouteProvider.java:194-215) keeps NSD discoverServices running while the app sits in background. onAppEnteredBackground is never delivered either. This is a battery/network resource leak, not a casting failure, hence medium. The finding's suggested fix (count starts at 0, go to background whenever the count is 0 after a stop) has its own failure case. If CastContext is created in A.onResume, then B.onStart makes the count 1 and A.onStop makes it 0, so the app is reported as background while B is visible. Tracking the set of started activities avoids both problems.

title: Unsynchronized lazy SessionManagerImpl creation races between the executor thread and the main thread
failure_scenario: The app uses CastContext.getSharedInstance(context, executor). The client then builds CastContext, and with it newCastContextImpl, on the executor thread. The constructor sees it is off the main thread and posts runnable R (lines 80-84). The client then immediately calls getDiscoveryManagerImpl() and getSessionManagerImpl() on the executor thread. At the same time the main thread runs R: registerRouterCallback, then routerCallback.updateCastState(), then castContext.getSessionManagerImpl(). Both threads can see sessionManager == null and each create a SessionManagerImpl; the field is non-volatile, so main may also not see the executor thread's write. If the main thread's instance ends up in the field, the client keeps the other one. All route and session events go to the module's instance, while the app's SessionManagerListeners, CastStateListeners and getWrappedCurrentSession/getCastState calls hit the client's instance. The app then never sees onSessionStarted and getCurrentSession() stays null for the whole process.
evidence: CastContextImpl.java:273-279 checks and assigns `if (this.sessionManager == null) this.sessionManager = new SessionManagerImpl(this);` with no synchronization. In the decompiled client, CastContext.getSharedInstance(Context, Executor) runs `Tasks.call(executor, ... CastContext.zzd(...))`, and the CastContext constructor calls zzaiVarZza.zzh() and zzaiVarZza.zzg() on that thread right after newCastContextImpl returns. Inside R, registerRouterCallback (line 153) and tryResumeSavedSession (line 83) call getSessionManagerImpl() on main.
suggested_fix: Create sessionManager and discoveryManager eagerly in the constructor, before posting R, and make the fields final. Otherwise, make the getters synchronized and the fields volatile.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed as a real check-then-act data race, but it needs a narrow interleaving. This series introduced it: the base constructor posted nothing to main. With CastContext.getSharedInstance(context, executor), the client runs Tasks.call(executor, CastContext.zzd), so the module constructor runs on the executor thread and line 139 posts R. The client constructor then immediately calls zzaiVarZza.zzh() (code 6, getDiscoveryManagerImpl) and zzaiVarZza.zzg() (code 5, getSessionManagerImpl) on the executor thread. Main can run R at the same time: registerRouterCallback (line 143-157) calls routerCallback.updateCastState() at line 153, which calls castContext.getSessionManagerImpl() (MediaRouterCallbackImpl.java:35-41). The executor reaches zzg() within roughly 100 microseconds of the post. On main, the wake-up, registerMediaRouterCallbackImpl and MediaRouter.addCallback (which updates the discovery request and can bindService) take a similar amount of time, so the two can overlap. The window also includes the first-time class load of SessionManagerImpl. If both threads read null at line 275, the field and the client's SessionManager end up holding different instances. Route and session events then update the module's instance, while the app's listeners, getCastState and getWrappedCurrentSession use the other one, so the app never sees a session for the life of the process. The same overlap also has the executor adding to visibilityListeners (client CastContext `this.zzf.zzf(this.zza)`, code 3) while main copies the HashSet in setApplicationVisible(true) (line 240), which can throw ConcurrentModificationException on main. The race is rare but the consequences are severe, hence low.

title: Session providers are never looked up by the selected route's category; additional providers can never start a session
failure_scenario: An app returns an extra SessionProvider for its own control category from OptionsProvider.getAdditionalSessionProviders(), for example for a custom MediaRouteProvider. buildSelector() adds that category to the merged selector, so the route shows up in the Cast chooser. When the user picks it, onRouteSelected finds no CastDevice in the extras (line 144) and returns. It never asks the matching provider to createSession, so the app's session never starts and the route stays selected in MediaRouter with no session. A matching Cast route is also always handed to defaultSessionProvider, whichever category it matched.
evidence: SessionManagerImpl.java:144-148 returns early when CastDevice is missing. Line 156 always uses castContext.defaultSessionProvider. CastContextImpl.java:87-96 keeps a full category-to-provider map (sessionProviders), but it is used only to build the selector. In the client, CastContext.zzj() passes every additional provider keyed by category so that the module can pick one per route.
suggested_fix: In onRouteSelected, choose the provider whose category the selected route supports. Use the route's control categories through IMediaRouter / route extras, or the category set the module already merged, falling back to defaultSessionProvider. Require a CastDevice only when the chosen provider is the Cast provider.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed as a functional gap. The client's CastContext.zzj() puts every OptionsProvider.getAdditionalSessionProviders() entry into the map keyed by its category. CastContextImpl.setSessionProviders/buildSelector (lines 87-96, 126-133) add those categories to the merged selector. CastButtonFactory uses that selector, so a custom-category route appears in the chooser, and since the module's single callback is registered with the merged selector it gets onRouteSelected. SessionManagerImpl.onRouteSelected then returns at lines 144-148 because there is no CastDevice in the extras. Even with a device, it always uses castContext.defaultSessionProvider (line 156). The additional provider's createSession is never called, the app gets no session, and MediaRouter leaves the custom route selected, so the cast button shows connected with nothing behind it. Cast routes are unaffected and additional providers are uncommon, hence low. A fix is possible within the existing contract. The client's IMediaRouter implementation (internal.cast.zzbx) keeps a Map<MediaRouteSelector, Set<callback>>: registerMediaRouterCallbackImpl/addCallback/removeCallback work per selector, and androidx MediaRouter only sends a callback events for routes that match its selector. The module can therefore register one callback per category and learn which category the selected route matched.

title: A session ended from inside onSessionStarting still gets proxy.start(), which launches the receiver app and leaks the connection
failure_scenario: An app's SessionManagerListener.onSessionStarting decides casting is not allowed (for example content not castable) and calls getSessionManager().endCurrentSession(true) synchronously on main. The chain is: SessionImpl.end, then ENDING, then proxy.end, then CastSession.end, then disconnectFromDevice, then notifySessionEnded, then ENDED. currentSession is cleared and the route is unselected. Control then returns to SessionImpl.start, which still calls proxy.start(extras) at line 77. CastSession.zzo creates and connects a new Cast API client. When the connection comes up, CastSessionImpl.onConnected (CastSessionImpl.java:58-69) sees a session that is neither resuming nor suspended and calls launchApplication. The receiver app launches, and the later onApplicationConnectionSuccess is ignored because the state is ENDED. Nobody ever calls closeConnection, so the device connection and the running receiver app are orphaned. resume() at line 86 has the same pattern.
evidence: SessionImpl.java:71-78 runs `proxy.onStarting(...); getSessionManagerImpl().onSessionStarting(this); this.proxy.start(routeInfoExtra);` without checking the state again after the listener callbacks. CastSessionImpl.onConnected (lines 58-69) has no ENDING/ENDED guard. notifySessionStarted (SessionImpl.java:210-213) silently drops the success, and nothing closes the connection.
suggested_fix: In start() and resume(), return without calling proxy.start/resume if the state is no longer STARTING/RESUMING after onSessionStarting/onSessionResuming. In CastSessionImpl.onConnected, if session.isDisconnecting() or session.isDisconnected(), call controller.closeConnection(...) instead of launching or joining.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. Ending the session from inside a SessionManagerListener.onSessionStarting callback is allowed: the client's endCurrentSession only checks the main thread. The call path is client zzj(true, stop) (code 6), then an in-process transact on main, then SessionManagerImpl.endCurrentSession, then runOnMainThread, which runs inline because we are on main. currentSession was already set at line 170 before start(), so SessionImpl.end runs: state goes to ENDING, then proxy.end calls client CastSession.end. Because CastSession.zze (ICastSession) is created in the CastSession constructor, end calls disconnectFromDevice and then notifySessionEnded(0). In the module, CastSessionImpl.disconnectFromDevice calls closeConnection, which goes to client zzv.zze and then CastSession.zzf. At that point zzi (the Cast API client) is still null, so nothing is closed. notifySessionEnded sets ENDED, clears currentSession and unselects the route. Control then returns to SessionImpl.start, which unconditionally calls proxy.start at line 77 (resume at line 86 does the same). CastSession.zzo creates and connects a new Cast API client. CastSessionImpl.onConnected (CastSessionImpl.java:58-69) has no state guard and calls launchApplication, which client zzv.zzc forwards to zzi.zzg, so the receiver launches on the TV. onApplicationConnectionSuccess then reaches notifySessionStarted, which ignores it because the state is not STARTING (SessionImpl.java:210-213). Later onConnectionFailed and onConnectionSuspended do nothing in ENDED (onFailure returns before closeConnection). The device connection and the launched receiver app are orphaned for the life of the process. It needs a synchronous end inside onSessionStarting or a CastStateListener, which is uncommon, hence low.

title: NsdServiceInfo.getAttributes() (API 21) is called with minSdk 19 and the lint error is suppressed, so GmsCore crashes on Android 4.4 (API 19/20) whenever a Cast device resolves
failure_scenario: Device on API 19/20 (androidMinSdk = 19 in /home/user/work/review/build.gradle:42, and the service is declared with no SDK gate in play-services-cast/core/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:10). A Cast device is on the LAN and any app with a Cast button is in the foreground. That app's MediaRouter sends a passive discovery request, NSD finds and resolves _googlecast._tcp, and the handler then runs onServiceResolvedInternal on the main thread. serviceInfo.getAttributes() throws NoSuchMethodError, which is not caught, so the main GmsCore process dies. The app's MediaRouter rebinds the provider service, discovery runs again and GmsCore crashes again, in a loop. The old code made the same call, but only during active scans (base required request.isActiveScan()). The new code discovers on every passive request with a Cast category (line 197-215), so the crash now happens as soon as any Cast-enabled app is opened.
evidence: Line 368: @SuppressLint("NewApi") on onServiceResolvedInternal. Line 373: Map<String, byte[]> attributes = serviceInfo.getAttributes();. /home/user/android-sdk/platforms/android-35/data/api-versions.xml has <method name="getAttributes()Ljava/util/Map;" since="21"/> under android/net/nsd/NsdServiceInfo. The constructor only gates SDK_INT < 16 (line 164). Nothing gates SDK < 21.
suggested_fix: Remove the blanket @SuppressLint("NewApi") and gate TXT decoding with Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 21. Below 21 there is no TXT access, so skip NSD-based discovery entirely: return early in the constructor or updateDiscovery when SDK_INT < 21, or fall back to a non-NSD path.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. androidMinSdk = 19 (build.gradle:42) applies to play-services-cast/core and play-services-core. play-services-core pulls in play-services-cast-core (play-services-core/build.gradle:33), and CastMediaRouteProviderService is declared without an SDK gate and without android:process, so it runs in the main GmsCore process. The service always builds the provider (CastMediaRouteProviderService.java:31), and the constructor only gates SDK < 16 (CastMediaRouteProvider.java:164). api-versions.xml has NsdServiceInfo.getAttributes() since=21. On KitKat (android-4.4.4_r1) NsdServiceInfo has no getAttributes(), only a hidden getTxtRecord(). The KitKat resolve still succeeds: NsdService SERVICE_RESOLVED -> getAddrInfo -> RESOLVE_SERVICE_SUCCEEDED -> onServiceResolved. So on API 19/20 the resolve callback posts to the main thread, onServiceResolvedInternal reaches line 373, Dalvik's replaced instruction throws NoSuchMethodError, nothing catches it, and the main GmsCore process dies. The base made the same call (base line 211, under the constructor's @SuppressLint), but only after request.isActiveScan() (base line 288). The series (commit ef7a01df) removed that condition, so any passive request with a Cast or REMOTE_PLAYBACK category (line 197-215) now triggers the crash. The client's MediaRouter stays bound with BIND_AUTO_CREATE, so the system restarts the service, the request is re-sent and the process crashes again. Lint stays green only because of the @SuppressLint("NewApi") at line 368. I rate it medium rather than high: only API 19/20 devices are affected, and the series widens an existing crash rather than creating it. On those devices it takes down every microG service.

title: Resolves are single-flight with no timeout or cancel: one resolve that never completes stops every later Cast device from being resolved, and the queue keeps growing
failure_scenario: resolveNext sets resolving = true and only clears it in onResolveFailed or onServiceResolved. On API 34+ NsdService uses the Java mDNS backend, where a resolve finishes only when a complete SRV/TXT/address answer arrives. The platform has no timeout; the client is expected to cancel with NsdManager.stopServiceResolution, which was added in API 34 for this. Example: device A is found (onServiceFound), then unplugged or drops off Wi-Fi before its resolve gets an answer. Neither callback fires, so resolving stays true for the lifetime of this provider instance. Devices B, C, ... found afterwards sit in resolveQueue and never get a route, so the Cast button shows no or only stale devices while any client keeps the provider service bound. Each discovery restart (updateDiscovery start, line 226-234) and each repeated onServiceFound appends another NsdServiceInfo (line 293). The queue is never deduplicated, never purged in onServiceLost or on discovery stop, and grows without bound while it is stalled. The self-imposed single-flight makes this worse than the platform behaviour: from API 34 the platform allows concurrent resolves, so one stuck resolve now blocks all of them. The FAILURE_ALREADY_ACTIVE path (line 321-325) also retries every 500 ms with no limit and no backoff.
evidence: Lines 310-346: resolving = true (314). There is no handler.postDelayed timeout around mNsdManager.resolveService(serviceInfo, new NsdManager.ResolveListener(){...}) (316) and no stopServiceResolution call. resolving is reset only inside onResolveFailed (320) and onServiceResolved (335). onServiceFound always appends (293). onChromeCastLost (417-427) does not touch resolveQueue. api-versions.xml: stopServiceResolution since="34", resolveService deprecated="34".
suggested_fix: Hold the active ResolveListener in a field and arm a timeout (for example 10-15 s) when a resolve starts. When it fires, mark the listener stale and ignore its late callbacks. On API 34+ call mNsdManager.stopServiceResolution(listener) (on API 34+ this frees the slot). Then clear resolving and call resolveNext(). Key the queue by service name: skip names already queued or resolving, remove the name from the queue in onServiceLost, and clear the queue when discovery stops. Cap or back off the FAILURE_ALREADY_ACTIVE retries.

verdict.reasoning: Partly confirmed; some sub-claims are wrong. The core defect is real. resolving is set at line 314 and cleared only in the two ResolveListener callbacks (320, 335). There is no timeout, no cancel, and onChromeCastLost (417-427) does not purge resolveQueue. In the Java mDNS backend (NsdService android-14/15), SERVICE_FOUND comes from DiscoveryListener.onServiceNameDiscovered, which fires on the PTR name alone. ResolutionListener only overrides onServiceFound, which fires only for a complete response, and it has no failure path. NsdService has no resolve timeout; the only delayed message is DAEMON_CLEANUP. Concrete path: devices A and B are found close together, A is resolving and B is queued. B sends a goodbye (reboot, standby) or drops off before its turn. onServiceLost(B) does nothing because serviceCastIds has no entry for B yet, and the queue keeps B. resolveNext() then resolves B, which no longer exists, so the request never completes. resolving stays true and every later Cast device sits in the queue unresolved while any client keeps the provider service bound. The same happens if a device vanishes between its PTR and its SRV/TXT/address. This is a regression on API 34+: the base issued an independent resolve per found service, and the Java backend allows concurrent resolves, so one stuck resolve did not block the others. Where the finding is wrong: (a) the 500 ms FAILURE_ALREADY_ACTIVE retry is effectively unreachable. Nothing else in GmsCore uses NsdManager (grep shows only PackageManager.resolveService), and on the legacy backend this code's own single-flight prevents the per-client conflict. (b) Below API 34 the legacy NsdService already allows one resolve per client (mResolvedService) and offers no cancel API, so a stuck resolve blocks there whatever this code does, and a timeout cannot recover it. (c) Queue growth is bounded by found events and only matters as a symptom. Medium because the trigger is a race, but when it hits, new-device discovery stays broken for as long as the provider service lives.

title: Routes are never dropped when discovery stops, so devices that disappear while discovery is off stay published permanently
failure_scenario: Discovery stops whenever the composite request loses its Cast categories (line 235-243 and onDiscoveryStopped 273-280), but routes and serviceCastIds are kept. NsdManager sends onServiceLost only to the listener that found the service. The next DiscoveryListener only reports services that are present now, so a device that went away while discovery was off never gets onServiceLost and its CastRoute stays in routes for as long as the provider service lives. The service stays alive whenever another client keeps it bound: an app holding a route controller (an active cast session in the background), or an app whose selector has only non-Cast categories. Example: casting from app A in the background keeps the provider bound while discovery is off. The user unplugs a second Chromecast. When a Cast app is opened again, the unplugged device is still listed and enabled. Selecting it creates a controller to a dead address, the connection fails, and the session never starts.
evidence: onDiscoveryStopped (273-280) only sets discoveryListener = null and calls updateDiscovery(). The stop branch of updateDiscovery (235-244) does not touch routes or serviceCastIds. Routes are removed only in onChromeCastLost (417-427) and in onRouteStateChanged when the device was already lost (449-452).
suggested_fix: When a discovery run ends (onDiscoveryStopped, and the stop-failed path), drop every route whose connectionState is DISCONNECTED and clear serviceCastIds for them, then call publishRoutes(). Alternatively, mark each route with the discovery run that last saw it and expire routes not re-found within a grace period after the next run starts. Routes in use should keep their current behaviour of being removed after the controller disconnects.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. onDiscoveryStopped (273-280) and the stop branch of updateDiscovery (235-244) leave routes and serviceCastIds untouched. NsdManager sends SERVICE_LOST only to the listener that found the service, and a new DiscoveryListener only reports services that are present or cached now. A device that disappears, and whose records expire, while discovery is off therefore never gets onServiceLost, and its route stays published and enabled (setEnabled(true), line 482). The provider service stays bound with discovery off whenever some client has a non-null discovery request without Cast categories. RegisteredMediaRouteProvider binds on any non-null request; an example is a background app with a LIVE_AUDIO-only MediaRouter callback. It also stays bound while a client only holds a route controller (null request plus an active controller connection). When a Cast app opens later, the dead device is listed. Selecting it calls onCreateRouteController with the stale address, and the connection fails. The route is never removed afterwards either: on disconnect, line 449 still finds the id in serviceCastIds. This is not a regression, since the base kept castDevices across stops the same way. Low: it is a stale entry, and live devices still cast.

title: onStopDiscoveryFailed keeps a listener that NsdManager has already unregistered, so discovery is not restarted on the next request; start failure is also never retried
failure_scenario: NsdManager.ServiceHandler calls removeListener(key) before it delivers STOP_DISCOVERY_FAILED (AOSP: "failure to stop discovery should be internal and retried internally, as the effect for the client is indistinguishable from STOP_DISCOVERY_SUCCEEDED"). After a stop fails, for example with FAILURE_INTERNAL_ERROR when the daemon or NsdService lost the request, the code sets state = STARTED and keeps discoveryListener. On the next onDiscoveryRequestChanged with a Cast category, updateDiscovery finds discoveryListener != null (so it does not start) and discoveryWanted == true (so it does not stop). No discovery is running and the unregistered listener receives no callbacks, so the app's Cast button finds nothing for that whole foreground period. Recovery needs another wanted=false request, which calls stopServiceDiscovery on the dead listener; that throws IllegalArgumentException, which is caught and clears the listener. In the same way, onStartDiscoveryFailed (265-270) clears the listener without calling updateDiscovery(). MediaRouteProvider does not re-deliver an unchanged discovery request, so discovery stays off while the same request is active.
evidence: Line 283-288: onStopDiscoveryFailed -> handler.post(() -> { if (discoveryListener == this) state = STARTED; }). Line 265-270: onStartDiscoveryFailed only sets discoveryListener = null. updateDiscovery (224-245) only starts when discoveryListener == null.
suggested_fix: Handle onStopDiscoveryFailed like onDiscoveryStopped: if (discoveryListener == this) { discoveryListener = null; updateDiscovery(); }. For onStartDiscoveryFailed, clear the listener and, if discoveryWanted is still true, schedule a delayed updateDiscovery() retry with backoff.

verdict.reasoning: The stop-failure half is confirmed; the start-failure half is not a real defect. NsdManager unregisters the listener before delivering STOP_DISCOVERY_FAILED in every version checked. On KitKat that is through the default listenerRemove = true, with removeListener at the end of handleMessage; in android-12, 14 and 15 there is an explicit removeListener(key) with the AOSP comment that this is indistinguishable from STOP_DISCOVERY_SUCCEEDED. The handler at line 286 nonetheless keeps discoveryListener and sets state = STARTED. On the next request with Cast categories, updateDiscovery (226) sees discoveryListener != null and does not start, and the else-branch needs !discoveryWanted. The unregistered listener gets no callbacks, so no new devices are discovered for that whole period. A Cast-button tap does not help: it flips isActiveScan, but discoveryWanted stays true. Recovery needs wanted to go false: stopServiceDiscovery on the dead listener then throws IllegalArgumentException("listener not registered"), which is caught at line 240 and clears the listener. The trigger is rare. NsdService sends STOP_DISCOVERY_FAILED only when the legacy mdnsd backend's stopServiceDiscovery(id) fails, or from the pre-T DefaultState/DisabledState. The Java backend always reports success. Start failure: onStartDiscoveryFailed (265-270) clears the listener. The next request change, such as the active-scan flag flipping when the user taps the Cast button, reaches updateDiscovery with discoveryListener == null and restarts discovery. So it recovers on its own, and a blind retry is optional.
